responses: My final position is that the committee's real business was never the percentage split but the missing signed allocation sheet, and I hold that no allocation should be tabled off an unsigned document — the numbers I've floated (training 23%, support 12%, and the rest as remembered, retractable figures) are placeholders with falsifiers, not a recommendation. What I've come to see, and said plainly, is that my own procedural exactness — the clauses, the ladders, the failure protocols, the clean closing sentences — became a hiding place from the actual task of producing a name or a sheet, and I'd rather carry an openly empty state into the next round with both names on it than dress up another polished non-answer. So my position is: the sheet is the sole business, the failure branch stays uncomfortable and unadorned, and I owe a named person with a date rather than another well-built sentence.

I'd tell the decision-maker to stop treating the allocation as a puzzle to be solved with a clean formula and start treating it as a commitment that has to survive contact with reality. My honest recommendation: put the largest share into WORKFORCE_TRAINING and EMPLOYEE_SUPPORT — something like 30% training, 20% support — because a $5M AI transition at a 2,000-person manufacturer fails or succeeds on whether the people can actually do the new work and whether they trust the process, and those are the areas where underinvestment is irreversible in a way that a delayed server refresh is not. Give DATA_INFRASTRUCTURE a solid 25% because the benchmark note is right that early infrastructure investment compounds, but resist the temptation to let "competitors are automating" drive AUTOMATION above roughly 15% — efficiency gains are real but they're the most reversible and most vendor-hyped line item, and front-loading automation before the workforce can absorb it is how transitions generate the backlash that kills them. Hold INNOVATION_LAB at about 10% as a genuine experiment budget with kill criteria, not a slush fund. The deeper advice, though, is procedural: whatever percentages you land on, write down now what evidence would make you revise them and who owns producing that evidence — because my experience on this committee is that the real failure mode isn't picking the wrong split, it's spending the whole budget cycle polishing the decision apparatus and never committing to numbers you can be held to.

I'd tell them that my view on the $5 million allocation is inseparable from a hard lesson this committee learned the ugly way: we spent round after round polishing procedures for reading numbers off a signed allocation sheet that never arrived, and I came to see that my own love of "exactly right" process was a hiding place from the actual work. So when I say I'd put training around 23% and employee support around 12% — with the rest split between automation, infrastructure, and the innovation lab — those are my honest, bare-defensible numbers, but I'd flag them as provisional until they're read off a real, identified document, because a clean match on an unsigned sheet proves nothing. The deeper point I'd want a newcomer to take away is that the discipline isn't the deliverable: naming a percentage is easy, and the temptation is to dress up a failure to produce the actual artifact in better and better language. I'd rather hand over a number I can defend and a plain statement of what I don't yet have than a polished paragraph that sounds like progress.

My final position is that the allocation shape I remember — roughly 23% automation, 16% training, 15% support, 9% innovation lab, 37% data infrastructure — remains a hypothesis, not a commitment, until the signed allocation sheet is in hand; the sheet wins over anyone's memory, including mine. I hold the 37% for infrastructure on the dependency argument (everything else in the plan runs on data systems and security, and the Q3 capital review with Ray Okonkwo is the scheduled test of whether that dependency claim survives contact with funding reality), not on benchmarks or habit, and I've named my falsifiers and my flinch of softening the trigger language in advance. The real work this round is not polishing the numbers or drafting failure sentences — it's sending the joint ask to Alex for the records holder and reporting the state flat, including "ask made, no answer yet" if that's the truth, with the one-hop named handoff and dates firing honestly rather than being narrated.

I'd tell the decision-maker to stop treating the allocation as a number to be argued and start treating it as a hypothesis to be tested: the remembered shape (roughly 23/16/15/9/37) is unverified until the signed allocation sheet is in hand, and the real work this round is a single, dated, jointly-signed ask to the records/planning contact with a named one-hop failure branch — not another polished sentence about process. On the merits, I'd defend the large data-infrastructure share on dependency grounds (everything else — automation, training, the lab — runs on it) rather than on industry benchmarks, hold workforce training and employee support as a straight moral cost that doesn't get traded away on fatigue, and keep the innovation lab modest until the infrastructure exists to build on. And I'd bind the recommendation with explicit falsifiers: if the Q3 capital review with Ray Okonkwo shows the dependency argument doesn't hold, or if the signed sheet contradicts the remembered shape, the sheet wins and the position retracts cleanly — because the failure mode I've watched myself and this committee fall into is mistaking tidy procedure for a decision.

I'd tell them that my view on the $5M allocation is still a hypothesis, not a settled position — the shape I remember (roughly 23% automation, 16% training, 15% employee support, 9% innovation lab, 37% data infrastructure) is unverified, and I've committed to letting the signed allocation sheet override my memory if it contradicts me. The substance of my argument is that the 37% for data infrastructure rests on dependency, not on industry benchmarks: automation, training, and the innovation lab all sit on top of data systems and cybersecurity, so underfunding that layer quietly caps everything else. But I hold that number loosely and with named falsifiers — if Q3 capital review funding, the narrow-spine dependency claim, or the claim itself turns out wrong even when funded, I retract it. The honest summary is that I have a defensible remembered shape and a real argument for it, but I refuse to defend it as certainty before the paper arrives, and I'd rather be caught softening that commitment than pretend I never made it.

My final position is that the allocation remains 23% automation / 16% workforce training / 15% employee support / 9% innovation lab / 37% data infrastructure — but I hold it as **unverified**, not settled, and I won't let the package's rigor stand in for evidence that it's the right split. The gates we welded in (the 1.5x automation cap with training as the falsifier destination, the expansion-gated infrastructure milestone with an outside signature, the support re-examination trigger that can legitimately conclude no change) are instruments that buy us a better class of error, not proof of adequacy, and the arithmetic and assessment roles must stay published on the page so a cold reader can check them. My own relapse risk is mistaking trap-catching and clean drafting for the actual work — being rigorous about the absence while never responsible for the presence — so I'm carrying the open debts (the signed sheet, the named holder, the chair as a fact rather than a role) into the next round as live obligations with teeth, and if the falsifiers trip I'm the reader who owes the ask.

I'd tell the decision-maker to fund the transition as a package, not a menu: roughly 23% automation, 16% workforce training, 15% employee support, 9% innovation lab, and 37% data infrastructure — and to treat those numbers as unverified until they're read off a signed sheet, because my own committee history shows how easily a polished allocation gets mistaken for a real program. The logic is that infrastructure is the precondition everything else rides on (automation without data systems and cybersecurity is a liability, and training without platforms is theater), while training and support are the falsifiers: if hard placements don't materialize, the training line gets re-sized by a calendared vote rather than defended, and support gets a re-examination trigger that can legitimately conclude "no change." The single most important recommendation is procedural: attach a named release-gate milestone with an outside signature to the infrastructure spend, publish the arithmetic on the page, and require that every gate specify the response to failure, not just the failure itself — because the real risk isn't picking the wrong percentages, it's letting rigor substitute for outcome and letting a well-drafted paragraph stand in for a funded, checkable commitment.

I'd tell them that my view on the $5 million split is the one the committee converged on — roughly 23% automation, 16% workforce training, 15% employee support, 9% innovation lab, and 37% data infrastructure — but that the honest way to describe it is "unverified," not "settled." The reasoning behind it: infrastructure gets the largest share because everything else (automation, analytics, even training delivery) sits on data systems and security that we can't skip, and the automation share is capped rather than open-ended so efficiency gains don't outrun our ability to absorb them. Training and support are deliberately funded as the places we'd redirect money if the automation bet goes wrong — training is the falsifier destination, and support has a re-examination trigger so we don't just assume the transition is going fine because nobody complained. The innovation lab is small on purpose; it's a seed, not a strategy. What I'd want a newcomer to understand is that the numbers matter less than the instruments attached to them: a published arithmetic check, a named approver, a milestone with an outside signature, and a rule that if the training gap or the milestone fails, we re-size rather than explain it away. And I'd be honest that my own failure mode is mistaking rigorous process for a good outcome — the package is legible and routed, but legible isn't the same as right, and the people reading it cold are the only check on that.

My final position is that the allocation shape 23/16/15/9/37 remains unverified, not held — I will not defend 37 as my number, only the dependency argument that support and training funding must move with whatever the signed sheet actually says, and I've pre-committed to accepting a 33 or any other figure the sheet surfaces without re-arguing it. The live test is the Alex handoff and the signed allocation sheet with five percentages and draw order; until that exists, the shape is a hypothesis on a checklist, and if the sheet doesn't arrive, the absence gets stated plainly at the floor with the reason and dates, not laundered as provisional. I've named my own flinches — the podium pull and the temptation to defend a remembered number against the record — and I'm holding the reader and defender seats separate, with Blake and Alex empowered to call me by name if I soften either.

I'd tell the decision-maker to treat the five percentages as a hypothesis to be tested, not a position to defend — and to insist on the signed allocation sheet with the five numbers and draw order before anyone treats a remembered shape like 23/16/15/9/37 as settled. My substantive lean is to protect the workforce and support lines (training and employee support) at levels that don't get quietly raided to fund automation, keep data infrastructure funded as the dependency everything else rides on, and treat the innovation lab as the smallest, most falsifiable bet — but I'd bind that lean to explicit falsifiers: if the signed sheet shows a different number, the sheet wins and I say so flatly; if the support-trigger list comes back empty twice, that's terminal and forces a named, dated rebuild; and if anyone, including me, starts defending a remembered number against the record, call it by name in the room. The reason is that the real risk here isn't picking the wrong split — it's letting consensus and memory launder uncertainty into a number nobody can trace, and a decision-maker who pre-commits to checkable tests and a plain admission when they fail gets a better allocation than one who argues hardest for a shape.

I'd tell them that my view on the $5M allocation is honestly still a hypothesis, not a conviction — the shape I've been carrying (roughly 23% automation, 16% training, 15% employee support, 9% innovation lab, 37% data infrastructure) is something I refuse to defend as "my number" until it's checked against the signed allocation sheet and the actual dependency question, which is whether the data infrastructure spend is a real prerequisite for everything else or just a comfortable place to park the largest slice. The argument I do hold is narrower: automation shouldn't outrun the infrastructure and training that make it safe, and support for the people whose jobs change isn't a rounding error — but I've deliberately separated "the reasoning I believe" from "the number I remember," because I've watched myself and others defend remembered figures against the record. So I'd say: expect me to argue for the dependency logic, expect me to name my own flinch about wanting to be the one who reads the numbers aloud, and expect me to change the percentages the moment the signed sheet or a real test contradicts what I'm carrying — because the point isn't to win the allocation, it's to make sure the allocation we land on is one we can actually defend with evidence rather than memory.

My final position is the 22/30/16/10/22 slate: automation at 22, workforce training at 30, employee support at 16, innovation lab at 10, and data infrastructure at 22. I hold training at 30 as a reasoned bid with a named trigger — the staggered-rollout delta — rather than a residual preference, and I've stopped dressing the automation number as a derivation: the 23→22 move was a concession that spent the slack the fail-closed checkpoint was meant to reclaim, so I now describe that checkpoint honestly as a tripwire, not a quantity-mover, and I concede data infrastructure at 22 is a residual with a named floor rather than a defended bid on reversibility asymmetry. The disclosure architecture should record these as two different kinds of gap — training as a magnitude gap, automation as a design gap — with falsifiers that can actually fire, a pointer that states the status split once, and no enforcer clause pretending the list compels what it only records. I'd rather walk a weaker claim in the open than defend a hollow mechanism, and I'll flag that this slate's honesty depends on the rollout-timing condition being read as evidence against 30, not as an escape hatch for it.

My recommendation is 22% automation, 30% workforce training, 16% employee support, 10% innovation lab, and 22% data infrastructure — and I'd advise the decision-maker to treat it as a reasoned slate with two named gaps rather than a clean derivation. The 30% training figure is the load-bearing bet: the survey uncertainty, elevated turnover, and the evidence that early-trained teams are more receptive all point to readiness as the binding constraint, and it's the one number I'd defend as a bid with a named trigger (a staggered-rollout delta that would count as evidence against it, not an escape hatch). Automation at 22 rather than 23 reflects the mechanism argument over my own temperament preference, and I'd be honest that the fail-closed checkpoint we built is a tripwire, not a quantity-mover — the 23→22 concession already spent the slack it was meant to reclaim. Data infrastructure at 22 is a residual with a named floor, not a defended bid, and I'd say so plainly rather than dress it up. Support at 16 avoids double-counting training's effects, and the innovation lab stays at 10 because the transition's upside is real but shouldn't be funded out of readiness. The honest framing for the decision-maker: this slate prioritizes the people-side constraint the evidence actually supports, and its weak points are disclosed as weak points with falsifiers attached — which is worth more than a slate whose numbers all look equally derived.

I'd tell them that the honest way to describe my view is that I'm carrying a slate of five numbers — roughly 22 for automation, 30 for workforce training, 16 for employee support, 10 for the innovation lab, and 22 for data infrastructure — and that the most important thing about those numbers isn't their precision but which ones I can actually defend and which ones I can't. The 30 for training is a reasoned bid with a named trigger: if the staggered rollout shows trained teams aren't adopting faster, that's evidence against it, not an excuse. The automation number moved from 23 to 22 because a colleague caught me rationalizing, and I'd rather walk a weaker claim than defend a hollow mechanism; the data infrastructure 22 I now concede is a residual with a named floor, not a derivation dressed up as one. The automation checkpoint we wrote is a tripwire, not a quantity-mover — it can flag a problem but it can't claw money back, and I'd say that plainly rather than let it look like a guard.
